lesson.title: Sharing electron pairs

steps.headline: Two atoms and one shared pair

lead.text: Atoms are steadiest when their outer shell is full. In the last lesson a sodium atom handed an electron to a chlorine atom, and both ended up with a full outer shell. A handover only works when one atom is keen to give and the other is keen to take. Hydrogen shows what happens when both atoms are short of the same thing.

A hydrogen atom has one electron, and its first shell has room for two. When two hydrogen atoms meet, neither can take an electron from the other without leaving its partner short. So they share. Each atom puts its electron into a pair that sits between the two nuclei, and each atom counts both electrons of the pair as its own. Both now count two electrons in the first shell, which is full.

A pair of electrons held between two atoms in this way is called a covalent bond. Both nuclei attract the shared pair at once, and that double pull keeps the atoms close together. A group of atoms held together by covalent bonds is a molecule.
Chlorine has seven outer electrons. Two chlorine atoms meet, and each puts one electron into a pair that the two atoms share, just as the hydrogen atoms did.

Chemists keep track of shared pairs with a simple picture called a Lewis drawing. Each atom is written as its symbol, and each shared pair is drawn as a line between two symbols. Hydrogen, H₂, is drawn as H–H, a single line for the one pair that its two atoms share.
A pair is two electrons, one from each atom, so every line stands for two electrons. The line is a way of recording that a pair is shared. The electrons themselves are not fixed on it.

afterFigure.text: Compare the two drawings. Hydrogen has one line, so one shared pair. Methane, CH₄, has a carbon atom in the middle with a line to each of four hydrogen atoms, so it has four shared pairs. A Lewis drawing tells you which atoms are joined and by how many pairs. It leaves out the real shape, since a methane molecule is not flat like the page. Treat the lines as bookkeeping.

lead.text: Two atoms can share more than one pair. An oxygen atom has six outer electrons, which leaves it two short of a full shell, so two oxygen atoms share two pairs between them. A link made of one shared pair is a single bond. Two shared pairs make a double bond, drawn with two lines, and three shared pairs make a triple bond, drawn with three.
Counting the shared electrons in a bond takes two moves. Count the lines, since each line is one pair. Then turn pairs into electrons, because each pair holds two.

A molecule often has several bonds, and the same counting covers all of them. Add up the pairs in every bond first, then turn the total into electrons. The next screen does this for carbon dioxide, where a carbon atom is joined to two oxygen atoms by double bonds.

steps.headline: Carbon dioxide has two double bonds. How many electrons are shared altogether?

workedSteps.text: A double bond is two shared pairs.
Each pair holds two electrons, so count in pairs first and then double.

steps.headline: Oxygen, O₂, has one double bond. How many electrons does it share?

workedSteps.text: A double bond is two shared pairs.

steps.headline: Electrons an atom keeps to itself

lead.text: Not every outer electron is shared. Oxygen in water has six outer electrons, and only two of them go into bonds, one in each of the two O–H bonds. The other four stay with the oxygen atom as two pairs. A pair of electrons that stays on one atom and is not shared is called a lone pair, and a Lewis drawing shows it as two dots beside the atom.
An atom's outer electrons come in two kinds. Some belong to shared pairs, which both atoms count. The rest sit in lone pairs, which only one atom counts.

afterFigure.text: In the picture, the oxygen in water carries two lone pairs and the nitrogen in ammonia carries one. Keep one thing straight when you count. A shared pair is counted by both atoms, but it is still only one pair in the molecule, so count it once when you are totalling the electrons of the whole molecule. Both atoms claiming it does not turn it into two pairs.

lead.text: Picture the shared pair in H₂. Each hydrogen atom uses it to fill its first shell, and the pair itself is a single pair.
Count the pairs in each bond first, then turn the total number of pairs into electrons.
Nitrogen gas, N₂, makes up most of the air. Its two atoms are joined by a triple bond.

lesson.orientation: Read single, double and triple bonds and distinguish shared electrons from lone pairs.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two neighbours both need a ladder to paint their houses this weekend. Neither can afford one alone, and neither has anything the other would swap for it. So they buy one ladder between them and keep it on the fence line. Both can reach it and use it, and each counts it as their own. The ladder also ties the two households together, since neither can take it away without the other noticing.

Some atoms strike the same bargain. The last lesson followed atoms that hand electrons over and so become ions. A handover needs an atom that wants electrons and another that will give some up. Two atoms that both want electrons have nobody to take from. They put a pair of electrons between them instead, and both count it towards their outer shell.
This lesson starts with two atoms and one shared pair. It adds pairs until the link between the atoms is double and then triple, and it ends with the electrons an atom keeps to itself.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count the shared and unshared electrons in a Lewis drawing.
intro.whyItMatters: Most of the molecules around you hold together by sharing electrons.

recap.keyIdea: A covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared by two atoms, and both atoms count it toward their shells. Each bond line is one shared pair, so the electrons in a bond are twice its pairs. Lone pairs stay with one atom.

blocks.text: Back at the fence, the ladder was the shared pair. You counted 4 shared electrons in O₂, 8 across the two double bonds in CO₂, 12 in ethene and 6 in N₂, taking pairs first and then doubling each time. You also met the electrons that stay on one atom as lone pairs.

recap.nextHook: Every molecule in this lesson has a formula such as H₂O or CH₄, which lists the atoms and leaves out the bonds. The next lesson shows how to read those formulas, including the numbers written in front of them.

questions.prompt: How many electrons are shared in the single bond of H₂?
hints: Count two electrons per shared pair.
A single line means one shared pair.
How many electrons make one pair?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One bonding pair contains two electrons.

questions.onCorrect: 2. One bond line is one shared pair, and a pair is two electrons.

misconceptions.feedback: One electron is only half a pair. Each atom adds one, so the pair holds both.

questions.prompt: How many electrons are shared in the double bond of O₂?
hints: Each bond line represents one pair.
A double bond has two shared pairs.
Multiply 2 pairs by 2 electrons per pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two pairs contain four shared electrons.

questions.onCorrect: 4. A double bond is two shared pairs, and each pair holds two electrons.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts one pair. A double bond has two pairs.

questions.prompt: How does a shared pair contribute to the two bonded atoms?
hints: Keep shell counting separate from the total electron count.

acceptedIdeas: Each atom counts the pair toward its shell
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A shared pair counts toward both shells while remaining one pair in the molecule.

choices.label: Each atom counts the pair toward its shell
Each atom receives two new extra electrons
Only the heavier atom counts the pair

questions.onCorrect: Both atoms count the same shared pair toward their shells, and it is still one pair in the molecule.

misconceptions.feedback: No new electrons are made. The same pair is counted by both atoms.
Both atoms count the shared pair, not just the heavier one.

questions.prompt: How many electrons are shared in the triple bond of N₂?
hints: Multiply the number of lines by two.
A triple bond has three shared pairs.
Multiply 3 pairs by 2 electrons per pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three shared pairs contain six electrons.

questions.onCorrect: 6. A triple bond is three shared pairs of two electrons each.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the pairs. The question asks for the electrons.

questions.prompt: NH₃ has one lone pair on nitrogen. How many nonbonding electrons is that?
hints: A lone pair is not a bond line.
The prompt gives one lone pair.
How many electrons make one pair?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A lone pair contains two electrons.

questions.onCorrect: 2. A lone pair is one pair of electrons that stays on a single atom.

misconceptions.feedback: A lone pair is two electrons, because it is a pair.

questions.prompt: Methane is drawn with four bonds on a flat screen. What can you infer from this Lewis drawing?
hints: Read bond connections without treating screen angles as measurements.

acceptedIdeas: It has four single C–H bonds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The diagram records four single bonds; it does not specify the real tetrahedral geometry.

choices.label: Its atoms must all lie in one plane
It has four single C–H bonds
Its bond angles must be 90 degrees

questions.onCorrect: The drawing shows four single C–H bonds. It is a bookkeeping diagram and does not show the real angles.

misconceptions.feedback: A flat drawing does not tell you the atoms lie in one plane.
The screen angles are a drawing choice, not a measurement.

questions.prompt: Each chlorine atom in Cl₂ starts with 7 outer electrons and puts one of them into the shared pair. How many outer electrons does each chlorine atom now count as its own?
hints: Each atom still counts the electron it put into the pair.
It also counts the electron its partner put in.
Add the partner's contribution to the starting count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 7 + 1 = 8: each atom counts its own seven plus its partner's one.

questions.onCorrect: 8. Each atom counts both electrons of the shared pair, which fills its outer shell. That is a covalent bond.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count before sharing. Each atom now also counts its partner's electron.
That adds both atoms' electrons. Each atom counts only its own shell.

questions.prompt: Ammonia, NH₃, is drawn with three N–H bond lines. How many shared pairs is that?
hints: What does one bond line stand for?
Count the lines.
One pair for each line.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each line is one shared pair, and there are three lines.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Each bond line is one shared pair.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts electrons. The question asks for pairs.
Each line is a pair of its own, so count every line.

questions.prompt: Why do we multiply the number of pairs by 2?

acceptedIdeas: Each shared pair contains two electrons

choices.label: Each shared pair contains two electrons
Each pair is shared by two molecules
A double bond always doubles the atoms

questions.onCorrect: Right: a pair is two electrons, so electrons are twice the number of pairs.

misconceptions.feedback: A pair is shared by two atoms inside one molecule, not two molecules.
Bonds do not change the number of atoms. They count pairs of electrons.

questions.prompt: Ethene, C₂H₄, has one double bond between its two carbon atoms and four single C–H bonds. How many electrons are shared altogether?
hints: Count the shared pairs in the double bond first.
Add the four single bonds, one pair each.
Turn the total number of pairs into electrons.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The double bond is 2 pairs and the four single bonds are 4 pairs: 6 pairs, so 12 electrons.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Count the pairs in all the bonds, then double.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of pairs. Turn it into electrons.
That counts only the double bond. Add the single bonds.
That counts only the four single bonds. Add the double bond.

questions.prompt: Water has two lone pairs on its oxygen atom. How many nonbonding electrons is that?
hints: What is one lone pair made of?
Count the pairs given.
Turn pairs into electrons.
questions.onCorrect: 4. Each lone pair is two unshared electrons.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the pairs. The question asks for the electrons.
